title: One look back
hookLine: he looks in on Yasodhara and the baby and does not wake them

cards: A doorway at night. A child's room, maybe, or a parent's, or someone you loved who was sleeping. You stand there a moment longer than you need to.
You don't go in. You don't say anything. You just look.
The prince has decided: tonight he will leave the palace, and he has told Channa to saddle his horse. But before he goes, there is one more door he has to stand in.
Down the corridor, Yasodhara sleeps, with their newborn son beside her.

teach.h: A HAND ON THE BABY'S HEAD.
teach.b: In the later telling, he opens the door quietly. A lamp is burning. Yasodhara is asleep on a bed strewn with flowers, her hand resting on the baby's head.
The prince wants, more than anything, to hold his son.

teach.h: IF SHE WAKES, HE CAN'T GO.
teach.b: But to lift the child he would have to move her hand, and she would wake. And if she woke, he knew he could not go. So he stays on the threshold.
The telling gives him one thought: when I have found what I'm looking for, I will come back and see my son. And he closes the door.
It's a tender scene, and one people argue about. Some readers today feel the ache of it: a husband and father walking out at night without a word. Buddhists hold the story in different ways.
Some see a great sacrifice, made for the sake of everyone, including this family.
Others say plainly that it's hard, and that the story's honesty about the cost matters.
The later stories add that Yasodhara, when she learns he has gone to live simply, gives up her own jewels and fine clothes, and that one day both she and Rahula will walk the same path.
Whatever you make of the leaving, the scene knows how the hardest goodbyes happen. Not with speeches. In silence, from a doorway, with a hand on the frame.
The Pali word for what he's choosing is nekkhamma, renunciation, and the story never pretends it's easy.

how: Buddhists tell the great going forth as the moment of renunciation, and many honor Yasodhara's part in it; the scene is often painted in temple murals, the prince standing at the door of the sleeping room.

o: a quiet promise to return to your family
a vow of silence kept through the night
giving up home life by choice, at a cost

games.q: who's in the doorway scene — tap the pairs.
p: asleep, her hand on the baby

s: the prince picked up his son before he left
he didn't: lifting him would have woken Yasodhara, and he knew he couldn't go then.
the telling has him promise himself to come back and see his son
when he has found what he's looking for.
Buddhists all see the leaving the same way
some see a great sacrifice; others name its cost plainly. the tradition holds both.

games.q: you're in the doorway. your wife is asleep, her hand on your newborn son's head. you long to hold him. what do you do?
o: lift the baby gently and risk waking her.
stay in the doorway and close the door quietly.
games.why: he stays on the threshold. if she woke, he could not leave, so he looks, and goes, meaning to come back.

practice: Think of a goodbye you couldn't say: someone who left, or someone you left, through a move, a breakup, a death, a friendship that just drifted.

Picture them as if you stood in a doorway looking in; you don't need to go in or fix anything, just look, and let whatever you'd have said be said silently now. Then let the door close gently, and come back to the breath.

wordCard.voice: Nekkhamma. Renunciation: the prince in the doorway, watching Yasodhara and his son asleep, choosing not to wake them.

orig.note: Pali: renunciation, the going out from home life. Sanskrit naiṣkramya.

carryVoice: Your line: the hardest leaving is quiet. He closed the door meaning to come back. Until tomorrow.

sources.ref: Nidanakatha (introduction to the Jataka): the look at Yasodhara and Rahula
